In view of the fact that the United States Congress subcommittee on appropriations will be voting further funds for the Garrison diversion unit by June 25, and in view of the fact that memos released this week by Congressman William Moorhead show that the United State bureau of reclamation has hidden facts from the State Department and the IJC, which is the group in which the Canadian Government has placed its confidence to protect Manitoba river systems from becoming sewers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway):

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF MORATORIUM ON SALES OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL AND TECHNOLOGY PENDING DECISION ON SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and relates to the conference held on the 19th of this month in London. It was a conference with countries exporting nuclear facilities and techniques at which Canada is reported as having been present. My question does not relate to the conclusions of this conference, but I should like to know if Canada has proposed a moratorium for at least a limited period on the sale of nuclear facilities and

techniques in order to provide time for the exporting countries to work out adequate safeguards?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF MORATORIUM ON SALES OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL AND TECHNOLOGY PENDING DECISION ON SAFEGUARDS

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF MORATORIUM ON SALES OF NUCLEAR MATERIAL AND TECHNOLOGY PENDING DECISION ON SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware the government has been making a concerted effort to ensure internationally that all nuclear co-operation be exclusively for peaceful purposes. It has had consultations to this end in various capitals, including the Prime Minister's discussions with world leaders. Canadian officials have been actively involved in discussions on this vital question. The discussions which have been reported in the newspapers should be seen in this context. The discussions are confidential and are concerned with common problems of the peaceful use of nuclear energy and the exchange of views at the working level.

subtopic: SALE BY GERMANY TO BRAZIL OF EQUIPMENT FOR FULL NUCLEAR FUEL CYCLE-POSSIBLE DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND CHANCELLOR

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SALE BY GERMANY TO BRAZIL OF EQUIPMENT FOR FULL NUCLEAR FUEL CYCLE-POSSIBLE DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND CHANCELLOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, granted that the meeting is confidential but this should not prevent the government of Canada indicating to parliament what the position is. Since reference has been made to the Prime Minister meeting with world leaders, I should like to ask whether he took up with the Chancellor of Germany the question of the contract which that country has made with Brazil to sell an entire nuclear fuel cycle, including fuel enrichment equipment and reprocessing facilities, a country that has not signed even a non-proliferation agreement. Did the Prime Minister discuss this matter with the Chancellor; or, if this matter did not come to the attention of the Prime Minister at that time, has Canada, since then, made any protest or representation to the government of West Germany on this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SALE BY GERMANY TO BRAZIL OF EQUIPMENT FOR FULL NUCLEAR FUEL CYCLE-POSSIBLE DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN PRIME MINISTER AND CHANCELLOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not discuss that particular contract with the Chancellor. I confess that it had not been brought to my attention, perhaps because it was not widely known at the time. But I discussed the general subject at length with the Chancellor and repeated to him the position I had taken with other European and world leaders, to the effect that increased Canadian safeguards would only be effective if other countries which had nuclear capabilities were willing to increase their own safeguards and that we should all be losers if the safeguards applied by one country were outflanked by the actions of other countries. That is the tone of the discussions I had with the Chancellor and, I repeat, with other leaders. We agreed generally that it would be in the interest of all if we could establish workable safeguards at the bilateral level and multilaterally. The conference in London, Mr. Speaker, is discussing this very type of thing, so that Canada is not alone in seeking to strengthen these safeguards.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I think the Prime Minister and Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree that the answers we have heard so far are in the nature of generalities. May I ask the Prime Minister a specific question about Canada's own attitude? Is Canada prepared to demand of South Korea, Argentina or any other country to which it is trying to sell a CANDU reactor this: that the recipient country will not acquire or buy facilities which can be used for the recycling of spent rods or plutonium made in atomic reactors without, at least, the approval of the appropriate international agency?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT COUNTRIES AGREE NOT TO ACQUIRE NUCLEAR RECYCLING EQUIPMENT PRIOR TO SALE OF REACTORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are asking for more than that. We are asking for undertakings from any countries which want to acquire nuclear technology or nuclear materials from Canada. We are asking them to undertake not to have any explosive device. The techniques the Leader of the Opposition has referred to are ones that can lead to the separation of plutonium and, eventually, to explosions, peaceful or otherwise. That is why we have made it clear that Canada wants the end result to be the assurance that there will be no nuclear explosions, and as far as we are concerned there is no such thing as a peaceful nuclear explosion.

subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT COUNTRIES AGREE NOT TO ACQUIRE NUCLEAR RECYCLING EQUIPMENT PRIOR TO SALE OF REACTORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of the subject, may I ask the Prime Minister if he can answer my question specifically, and not repeat generalities, the general demand that there be no atomic explosions? subtopic: PROPOSAL THAT COUNTRIES AGREE NOT TO ACQUIRE NUCLEAR RECYCLING EQUIPMENT PRIOR TO SALE OF REACTORS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. I have it indicated here that Korea has undertaken the obligation to the international community not to develop or acquire nuclear explosives of any kind. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the minister's statements both inside and outside of this House expressing his government's support for family planning as being one answer to the abortion problem in this country, would the minister explain to the House why it is that the position of director of family planning services in his department has remained unfilled and vacant for one year; and further, why it is that in his own budget family planning funding has not increased even in accordance with inflation, let alone with regard to the need for new programming in family planning?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: FAMILY PLANNING-REASON FOR FAILURE TO FILL POSITION OF DIRECTOR AND REDUCTION OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position which the hon. member is referring to comes under the jurisdiction of the Public Service Commission, which has tried to hire the most competent specialists. Up to now, it has failed in its efforts to find a suitable person from within the public service to fill this position. We have therefore been compelled to place ads in news media, and I am advised now that this position should be filled within the next few days.
As to the second part of the question, may I remind the hon. member that the estimates for the family planning program were very considerably increased only last year. The rate of increase is in fact much higher than those of the cost of living or the Gross National Product. It is dangerous to limit an analysis simply to the budget of this program. One must also take into account the contributions the federal government is paying through the public assistance program, the hospital insurance program, the medical assistance program to provincial family planning and health and welfare programs generally. As a matter of fact, when one takes into account federal government contributions in all these areas, one readily realizes that the increase in federal government contributions have been very appreciable indeed over the past few years.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (for the President of the Treasury Board) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology

speechtext:
that Bill C-63, to amend the Olympic (1976) Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is almost two years since this House was asked to give its approval to the Olympic (1976) Act. The proposed legislation which is before parliament today is intended to provide the necessary authority for the introduction of additional programs which will assist the Olympic organizing committee in the financing of the Olympic Games which are now but 13 months away. I believe it would be helpful for all hon. members if, in introducing this legislation, I were first to review the major considerations which were the subject of public attention when the Olympic (1976) Act was before the House. I will state them briefly and then come back to each one in greater detail.
The first point to recall is that at the time of enactment of enabling federal legislation which would permit the operation of three revenue-generating programs, assurances were received that the federal government would not be asked for any direct financial contribution to the 1976 summer Olympic Games. Hon. members will recall that these assurances were received from the government of Quebec, the city of Montreal and the Olympic organizing committee and were tabled in this House on February 2, 1973. The revenue-generating programs which were included in the Olympic (1976) Act are the Olympic coin program, the Olympic stamp program and the Olympic lottery. The legislation also provided that the Olympic Corporation for taxation purposes would be deemed to be a registered Canadian amateur athletic association, so that donations by individuals and corporations could be deducted from taxable income.
The second major point, as stressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his statement of February 2, 1973, is that although the federal government would not be granting funds directly to the Olympic Corporation, federal involvement in the 1976 Olympics would go beyond the provision of enabling legislation: this support would be provided through the medium of regular programs operated by various federal departments and agencies. It was realized at that time that additional funds would be necessary, particularly for broadcasting and security requirements.

Mr. Speaker, as an introduction to the debate on the legislation before us, I would like to review the provisions of the first Olympic act, and discuss the developments that have taken place since its adoption.
The Olympic (1976) Act provided for the sale of $5 and $10 coins and for the issuing of stamps and related postal goods commemorating the Olympic Games. It also authorized the creation of a national Olympic lottery. The olym-
Olympic Financing
pic coin program became mammoth undertaking, by far the most audacious of the kind ever entered upon. Within a few months, Canadian Olympic coins were put on the market in fifty-five countries. However, there has been a softening demand for such coins as a result of world wide recessionary trends, the uncertain climate regarding money prices, and the somewhat cloudy future of the games being held in Montreal following the much publicized strikes and delays that took place. On the basis of past experience, officials responsible for the Olympic coin program now predict net receipts of at least $100 million, which will greatly help towards the financing of the games. Now if we consider the Olympic stamp program, we note that the sale of these stamps, which bear a surcharge destined for COJO, has recently received greater support from the public. This may be a sign of renewed interest shown by Canadians in the 1976 summer Olympic Games. We remain optimistic about the possibility of obtaining $10 million from this program. As you know, the success of the Olympic Lottery has gone beyond all expectations. COJO now expects net receipts from this program to exceed $200 million.

Mr. Speaker, considered together, it is expected that the programs which were authorized by parliament through passage of the Olympic (1976) Act should realize net revenues of approximately $350 million. These estimates would not only meet but would exceed by some $50 million what was originally planned to be generated by these programs. As hon. members will recall, the 1976 Olympic Games were planned to be self-financing. It is now apparent that the increase in expenditures will exceed the increase in planned revenues. The federal government is seeking parliament's approval of legislation that will establish further programs designed to provide additional revenues for the Olympic organizing committee. [Translation]
The legislative measure we are considering today involves two elements: first, the issue of $100 gold coins bearing the date 1976 and commemorating the Olympic Games; second, granting the Olympic Games Organization Committee proprietary rights in trade marks and copyrights.
According to COJO and the city of Montreal, the production and sale of a $100 gold coin constitute basically a complementary program to the existing one concerning silver coins. The potentialities of the gold coins program have been under consideration by experts who reached the conclusion that numismatists and collectors-in Canada as well as in other countries of the world-would be deeply interested in them. According to these experts, the factors that justify the purchase of a gold coin vary basically from those that justify the purchase of a silver coin. They feel that the sale of gold coins for the Olympic Games will not reduce the sale of silver coins. The Olympic Games Organization Committee which has requested the establishment of this program, is convinced that such a program will serve as a valuable contribution to the games financing. As for the silver coins, all costs related to production, marketing, and distribution will be deducted from the sale amounts and the net proceeds will be paid to COJO.

Mr. Speaker, the clause of the bill concerning trade marks and copyrights aims at providing COJO with the protection which is necessary to carry out its licencegranting program. The advertising value of such an important event as the Olympics makes it advisable to associate a wide range of products and services with this event. This is why this program is likely to be an important source of extra revenues for COJO. Essentially, the clause of the bill dealing with trade marks and copyrights provides COJO with a protection similar to the one EXPO 67 enjoyed. [English]
I have spoken of how the federal government has been, and is, ready to support the Olympics by introducing the necessary enabling legislation for the revenue-generating programs of the Olympic organizing committee. However, Mr. Speaker, the support of the federal government goes beyond this. In fact, the support provided to the 1976 Olympic Games by the federal government through normal programs involves some 30 departments and agencies and is expected to amount to approximately $130 million. I would like to review briefly, for the benefit of hon. members, the highlights of this support.
The federal government, through the Department of National Health and Welfare, has increased the amount of assistance that has been available to Canadian athletes either through grants to national sports governing bodies or via the student scholarship program. The level of this support now stands at close to $2 million for this year.

In addition to providing assistance to our athletes, Canada as host country is also responsible for ensuring an adequate supply of competent officials and judges. Thus, funds are also being made available for the training of qualified Canadian officials of international calibre. In addition, Canada Manpower centres have made special arrangements to find the literally thousands of workers that are already needed or will be needed in the months to come. This support, plus the provision of other hiring and registration services, will cost the department an estimated $1.6 million.
Furthermore, under the auspices of the Department of the Environment, and through the Department of Public Works, work has been undertaken at Kingston, Ontario, to provide a breakwater and to deepen the harbour that will be used for the Olympic sailing events. This work, costing approximately $800,000, is virtually completed and the sailing facilities will be used for a major international regatta this summer. In addition, consultations have been carried out and advice has been provided by the Department of Transport on the applicable marine regulations and safety requirements. Complete weather information will be provided by the Department of the Environment for all Olympic activities.
Planning is continuing by the RCMP, provincial and municipal police forces and the Department of National Defence of security arrangements for the Olympics. The assignment and sharing of tasks under the security plan is the result of close consultations between the federal government and the provincial and municipal governments.

The total cost of federal government support for security will be $90 million, of which approximately $45 million will be provided through supplementary funds. This will involve approximately 10,000 men primarily from the RCMP and the Department of National Defence. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, traditionally Olympic Games have been more than a simple athletic competition. They are a very original way of gathering thousands of young people and spectators from all nations in the world who come to share their experiences and make known their national customs and culture. Simultaneously with the Olympics will be held a cultural festival which will illustrate for the many visitors who will be in Canada the authenticity of our own national personality. Therefore, cabinet has approved a $1 million grant to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) to allow for travel and accommodation expenses of all Canadian artists who will participate in that festival.
You will recall that the federal government will spend $25 million as supplementary funds for the CBC which will be the host broadcaster during the Olympics. Broadcasting all Olympic events will cost about $56 million. The difference will be paid by COJO and foreign broadcasters.
At the request of COJO, the National Film Board will produce the official film of the 1976 Olympic Games. The NFB will spend $300,000 out of its budget for that purpose. Eventually, the NFB will use that material for social, cultural and educational purposes.

Mr. Speaker, it is evident from the highlights I have cited that there is a broad range of federal activity in support of the 1976 Olympics. The magnitude and scope of these activities represents a significant measure of support for the games. In addition to the federal support that I have just outlined, and in addition to the programs which have already been made possible by parliament, we are seeking the approval of the House today for further revenue-generating programs. I would like to take this opportunity to announce that the government is considering similar proposals to support the 1978 Commonwealth Games which will be held in Edmonton.
Barely a year from today, Mr. Speaker, the attention of the people of Canada and, indeed, of the world will be focused on the Olympic Games. We will be cheering our athletes on to what will undoubtedly be our most successful venture ever into international competition of this calibre. It will be a time to be proud of our athletes, their trainers, coaches and managers and of the effort and sacrifice that their successes will require. Today I call on the members of this House and on all the people of Canada to support this legislation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is appropriate that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) made the statement on the Olympics because it was he, when he was president of the Treasury Board, who assured this House two years ago that no further legislation would be introduced for the purpose of aiding the 1976 Olympics. It is ironic how things change on the other side.
Allow me to begin, Madam Speaker, by reiterating this party's support for the 1976 Olympics in Montreal and
June 20, 1975

Kingston. We believe now, as we did when the original financing bill was passed, that there is a great opportunity for Canada and Canadians to benefit in hosting this prestigious international event. Although they will be held in Montreal, we all realize that the Olympics belong to-Canada. They can reflect Canada to the world and bring to Canada a sense of pride and unity.
While I admit our complete support of the Olympics and the benefits that will accrue to Canada and Canadians through world advertising, tourism, youth participation and bringing together the many countries in unity, at the same time I do not hesitate to point out that I intend to remain the watchdog for the taxpayers of this country and I shall be the first to criticize any questionable expenditures as a result of federal funding. It is with this in mind that I view the opportunity to speak on behalf of our party with mixed feelings. I, naturally, wish the Olympic committee every success in its endeavours to bring to the Olympics the unique principle of self-financing. Like many Canadians, however, I am deeply concerned about the too common eleventh-hour approach to the growing problem of Olympic financing and the shroud of secrecy that continues to surround this whole affair. In this respect I refer not only to COJO in Montreal but to the federal government in whose hands the final responsibility rests whether we like it or not.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has constantly stated that the Olympic Games are not the responsibility of the federal government and that the financing of the Olympics is not the responsibility of the federal government. Indeed, the Prime Minister did not consider any part of the Olympic program to be the responsibility of the government. But how can you take these statements seriously? Consider these facts: the Prime Minister accepted responsibility, on behalf of Canada, back in 1969, as shown by the letter written to the International Olympic Committee which has been made public. No less than six federal departments are involved in some way in helping with costs. The federal government introduced the original Olympic financing bill, Bill C-169, under which help was made available to COJO. As well, it is well known, as the minister just suggested, that the government has helped the games and will continue to help them with grants made for items such as security, immigration, health, CBC coverage-I understand the CBC will be the host broadcaster-CMHC construction and many other items. These grants will total well over $100 million.
The help the government has given the games does not bother me; I do not think it bothers anyone. What really bothers me is the government's deception, its misrepresentation, its statements such as that the federal government will not assume responsibility for the games. The Prime Minister said on June 28, 1973, that there will be no special assistance, no special financial aid from the federal government to Montreal or to COJO for the holding of the Olympic Games; it is not the federal government's responsibility. He has said that repeatedly. But he wrote the letter of acceptance on behalf of Canada, and now half the cabinet is involved in helping the Olympic cause.
That is not what bothers us. What troubles us is the way this government has behaved. It says that it is keeping its
Olympic Financing
hands off the Olympics. That is, or was, the official policy. It has been secretive and refused to give information. It has not told members of parliament who have raised questions in the question period, or the media, where it stands and where Montreal stands. At least, it has not done this officially. Any help which has been given has been given in secrecy right from the beginning. As I say, this air of total secrecy which has surrounded the entire Olympic matter has been raised many times in this House, in editorial comments and by the media in all parts of this country. As the time available for Olympic fund raising is fast drawing to a close, the government should come clean with the Canadian people.
Most of us realize that Olympic coin sales have not met expectations. They are lower than we expected them to be only one year ago. Actually, less than $25 million has been realized from coin sales, or less than 10 per cent of projected revenue. Therefore, I was amazed to hear the Minister of Public Works say that the program was a success.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) ACT AMENDMENT COVERING ISSUE OF GOLD COINS
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) ACT AMENDMENT COVERING ISSUE OF GOLD COINS
speechtext:
How can he suggest it is a success? Two years ago he assured us, in this House and in committee, that the coin program will realize $250 million. Less than one year remains before the Olympic Games are to begin and coin sales remain disappointing. Only 10 per cent of projected sales have been realized. It is worth considering: that if the silver bullion which is being used for the minting of Olympic silver coins had been sold in bulk after the rapid increase in silver prices, we could have realized some $200 million in profit and turned the money over to the Olympic committee. This would have avoided the frustration and costs of the coin program, a program which has been little but an exercise in frustration for the last two years.
It is time to examine this dismal failure which has resulted partly from inflationary trends, labour strife, the unexpected rise in silver prices and from other troubles in our economy. Part of the trouble stems from factors which have led the economy to perform less well than the government said it would perform. Also, the coin program's sad showing results from the government's lateness in bringing before parliament the original financing bill. We asked the government to introduce the bill. We did not know what its contents would be; we only knew that a bill would be introduced and repeatedly asked the government to bring it forward. But the government kept delaying its introduction until it was obviously too late to do much good.
The coin program also failed because it was handled ineptly by the Post Office. I have nothing but sympathy for the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) who inherited responsibility for the coin program from his predecessor. Incidentally, I am happy to see the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) sitting in his seat. As I say, I sympathize with the Postmaster General who inherited this fiasco-a fiasco which is only equalled by that of the Department of Transport. The Postmaster General is given ultimate responsibility for the Olympic coin and stamp program.
Of course, I should refer not only to the deficiencies of the Olympic coin and stamp program but to the over-all
June 20, 1975

Olympic Financing
inefficiencies within the Post Office which are partly the cause of the large deficits now being incurred by COJO. No wonder the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is being plagued with problems to do with tainted meat. I sympathize with the Postmaster General; it is too bad that he had to inherit a department which was in such a sad condition. I also sympathize with Montreal and the province of Quebec as the city and province will be responsible for an ultimate deficit of some half a billion dollars when the two-week Olympic event is over. Let me add this is not my personal opinion. Montreal and Quebec have the present Liberal administration to thank for the deficit. They have the Liberal administration to thank for what happened with regard to the financing bill and for all the troubles which have beset the Olympics from day one.
Having said this, let me return to what happened some two years ago after the original financing bill was passed by parliament. It was passed only after needed and important amendments had been introduced by my party. As you will recall, the Canadian people were assured by the Prime Minister, members of the cabinet, the mayor of Montreal and COJO that parliament would not be asked again for further support or assistance by way of new legislation or funds. Of course, the good mayor of Montreal has a reputation for making pertinent and unforgettable statements. Perhaps his most famous comment was that the Olympics are no more likely to have a deficit than a man is likely to have a baby. I understand that the mayor has been in the presence of Dr. Morgentaler in the last few weeks!
In all seriousness, I commend the brilliant achievement of the mayor of Montreal. He obtained for Montreal and Canada the Olympic Games in the teeth of strong opposition from countries such as the United States and the Soviet Union. This deed is worthy of the mayor and we ought to give him credit for bringing the Olympics to Canada. It is sad that because this government has failed to act, or has acted in secrecy, the Olympics are now in financial trouble.
Be that as it may, although the government assured all parties in the House that we should not be asked to consider new legislation, we are considering, in this eleventh-hour crisis, Bill C-63. I suggest, at the same time, that but for the inability of the Mint to strike all Canadian coinage with an Olympic symbol-I am referring to nickels, dimes, quarters, and so on-we would have before us a much more comprehensive bill asking us to grant the Olympic committee a partial seigniorage on this coinage; but that is not possible.
This bill, at first glance, seems to be simple and harmless. It seems to deal with nothing more than gold pieces, the registration and copyright of symbols, and trade marks. But it is vague; it says little about the specific issues we are interested in and many between-the-line questions will need to be answered before my party will be willing to agree to passage of the bill.

speechtext: Filibuster!

subtopic: OLYMPIC (1976) ACT AMENDMENT COVERING ISSUE OF GOLD COINS
speechtext:
For example, we do not know the percentage of the gold to be used in these coins, the number of coins that are to be minted, or the timetable for minting and distributing them. We do know that the Mint is presently behind schedule in the minting of the silver coin series. In fact, we wonder whether the gold coins will be minted and sold prior to the games. If not, will there be a market for these coins after the games are over? Indeed, is there a market for them now?
We were told there was a market for $450 million worth of silver coins. We questioned the government on that matter. I do not want to be in the position of saying "we told you so", but we persistently questioned the minister on this matter and he assured us there was a market. Are we to believe there is a market for the gold coins, or is it to be put into the same category as the silver coins and end up at the end of the year with 10 per cent of the total projected sales?
I believe the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) received instructions some time ago-in fact, before this bill was even presented-to purchase for the Mint special equipment for the sole purpose of minting gold coins. We do not know anything of the sale projections. Most important, there is no real definition as to the price of the gold that will be used in these coins. The bill simply reads, and I quote from clause 3:
11.1 With respect to any gold held by or on behalf of the Minister of Finance for the exchange fund account that is used in the production of gold Olympic coins, the Minister of Finance shall, for the purposes of this act and the Currency and Exchange Act, determine the selling price of that gold on the basis of the market price of the gold when the selling price is determined.
When will the selling price be determined? What will be the date? When will the delivery of the gold be made to the Mint? What is the precise definition of "market price" as it reads in the bill? Is this to be assumed as a free market price, or will the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) determine a figure between the book value, which I believe is $42, and the free market value which is some $160? These are very important questions.
We realize that we must move quickly with the passage of this bill. It is already too late. However, the answers to these questions are not in the bill. We cannot just sit here, close our eyes and open the door to any suggestion by the government to suddenly, at the eleventh hour, bail out COJO. We want COJO to succeed and we want the Olympics to succeed. However, as an opposition we have a responsibility to ensure that these bills are passed properly and that these very pertinent questions are answered. There are many more questions. I will not dwell on them at this time because this bill will be moving into committee stage. I know that some of my colleagues will be speaking on it this afternoon.
In his statement, the minister had the audacity to mention aid to athletes in the Olympic Games. That is a complete joke. They cannot

I suggest that is a result of the fact that the media drew attention to this. I am glad the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has raised the point at this time. For the past year or two Treasury Board has been recommending to private industry that athletes training for the Olympic Games be given leave of absence with pay. However, one or two months ago Treasury Board sent out a typewritten, official document stating that the policy of Treasury Board was not to give leave of absence with pay to anyone working for the federal government. It came out in the media that this is a contradictory situation. We were all very happy with the statement that Treasury Board would be kind enough to give three months off to these people who are more than athletes when it comes to international competition; they are roving ambassadors for Canada; they spread more goodwill for this country than a lot of politicians.
Why does this bill, for example, contain a comprehensive outline of the registration of trade marks, symbols and proprietary rights? The minister dwelt on this matter; he stated it was very important for COJO to have these trade marks registered and copyrighted. I do not understand why it has to be in a federal bill. Every industry, business and corporation registers their trade marks under the Trade Marks Act; they register and have copyright of their trade marks, symbols, and so on. Perhaps when we get to committee it will be explained why this part of the bill is even before the House.
What will be the accounting process to parliament on this bill and, indeed, on the over-all financing of the games, particularly when funds are derived as a direct result of federal participation? I repeat, the time has come for this government to come clean with the people of Canada. Because the majority of the funds for the Olympics are in fact derived by way of federal participation, the government must be accountable for how and where the moneys go that are derived as a result of federal assistance.
The CBC, as host broadcaster, has a budget of over $50 million to be used for facilities that will become obsolete on the closing day of the Olympics. I have not just picked this out of the air; it is on record. The president of the CBC said that there are no plans for the facilities being built specifically for the televising of the Olympics in Montreal. If they could be utilized after the games, that would be fine. However, this will be a white elephant in the middle of Montreal. As it now stands, $25 million of
Olympic Financing
this budget is a direct federal grant. I suggest that this figure will increase.

When touching on the subject of the CBC I would be remiss if I did not bring up once again the name of Marvin Josephson of International Famous Agency of New York city, hired by COJO for $375,000 plus to obtain television rights after-I emphasize the word "after"-the $25 million agreement had been completed with the American Broadcasting Corporation. He did nothing then and has done nothing since, and it would be a sad precedent if the Olympic Games from Canada were, for the first time, not to be carried in Europe over the European television network. As it now stands, even with this crackpot agent from New York, COJO and the European television network are far apart. It seems to me they will not reach the $25 million figure they were asking; the network is offering somewhere between $5 million and $10 million. This is just one typical example of the unbelievable waste of money which takes place on a regular basis.
We see the Montreal city council authorizing the construction of Olympic facilities, using moneys obtained from federally-sponsored programs, without offering contracts for public tender. Yet we sit idly by. The time is long overdue for the federal government to demand accurate accounting with respect to the over-all financial administration of the Olympics, particularly as such matters relate to the Olympic financing legislation passed by parliament. As a nation which has committed itself to the Olympics in Montreal, we cannot go on passing legislation freely without even a budget setting out the use of the funds derived from such legislation.
The answer we get from COJO is that a budget will not be available until the books are closed. This is not good enough, not if we are to continue to open our legislative doors in support of Montreal. The least we should ask for is an accounting showing where federal moneys go and how they are spent. I am not suggesting we become involved in the administrative processes of COJO and the Olympic committee, but we should certainly have an accounting as to what is happening to the money which comes directly from the government, regardless of what the cabinet says. The air of secrecy which has surrounded the entire Olympics program since its inception, including the arrangements for the letting of the television contracts and the practice of closed bidding on other contracts, must be dispelled and the indifferent attitude of the Prime Minister must be changed so that Canadians may be able to lend their complete support to the 1976 Olympics. Only then will they see clearly the many benefits which will accrue not only to our youth but to our entire country.
Thousands of athletes from virtually every country in the world have spent months, and indeed years in preparation for this event; thousands of Canadians have been making the same preparations, and all are looking forward to becoming a part of the spirit of the games. In accepting the application for the 1976 Olympics in Montreal, the Prime Minister accepted for all of Canada. Yet his hands-off policy has done little to ensure national confidence in this event, and without further assistance financial disaster is obviously apparent. His band-aid, patchwork approach to our national problems is again exemplified in

his approach to the inevitable in the Olympic financing bill. All cost-saving recommendations of the past, such as the very practical suggestion of decentralization, have been ignored. As early as January 16, 1973, I stated in this House:
I believe that Montreal is the city best able to cope with the multitude of problems that would be faced when staging the games in Canada. However, because of the costs and added possible benefits to our country, we should consider partially decentralizing the games somewhat along the lines of the Munich Olympics which in fact took place in as many as seven different cities, one as far away as 550 miles from Munich.
Such a concept, if adopted, would have utilized existing facilities, spread the Olympics across Canada and made them available to thousands more Canadians. In addition, it would have reduced over-all costs considerably. If the House is to approve further funding, the time has come when we should be given authority to examine the Montreal Olympic program and make recommendations as to cost-saving methods before it is altogether too late. Had the government listened to my suggestion as to the decentralization of the games and advised Montreal that, while the heart of the Olympics should be kept in that city, other events should be held in centres around the country where facilities already exist, we would not find ourselves in the financial difficulty which is now apparent.
To those critics who tell us this is not in accordance with the rules of the International Olympic Committee, let me say that when the president of the IOC, Lord Killanin, was here in Canada some six weeks ago I had the opportunity to spend some time with him; he was aware of our suggestions with regard to decentralization and, as a matter of fact, he told me it was his hope that in future Olympiads the concept of decentralization would be followed because, as we all know, the Olympics have become far too large and costly for any single city. Unfortunately, of course, there is unlikely to be decentralization at the next Olympics because they will be held in Moscow, and Moscow, as part of a propaganda effort, will stage the games in the city alone and they will probably be the biggest and most costly ever held. But they will be paid for by the government.
It is regrettable that the government has chosen to ignore all such suggestions in the past, because it now finds itself in the position which can only be described as desperate. The new plan outlined in Bill C-63 certainly has merit and will provide new resources for COJO, but I can assure the minister that while I am as anxious as he is to ensure financial success for the 1976 Olympics, I am equally anxious to scrutinize carefully the expenditure of the taxpayers' dollars-and these are taxpayers' dollars, whatever the hon. gentleman says-as well as moneys derived from federal bills such as the one before us.
Before coming to an end, Madam Speaker, and realizing that we are to be blessed in this debate with words of wisdom from the New Democratic Party, I should like to go back briefly to February 2, 1973, when the NDP spokesman on Olympic matters stated, and I quote from page 899 of Hansard for that date:
My party approves the concept of the issuing of special coins and stamps. We wish our first Olympic Games every possible success as a potential great moment in the history of our nation.

That was back in 1973. We all know they went on to oppose everything and anything regarding the Olympics from then on. I look forward to hearing a renewed stand on Bill C-63 today.
Having said all this-and I might note that several of my colleagues will be adding further comments concerning outstanding questions which arise from this bill-I would assure the House that it is our intention to vote for this bill at second reading and pass it on to the committee stage. However, I must make it abundantly clear that unless we receive a clear explanation regarding the many unanswered questions and discrepancies surrounding not only this bill but the over-all financing of the games-and they go hand in hand-unless an up to date budget is made available, and unless we have an opportunity to question several key witnesses in committee, such as the director of the coin program who I was happy to see has received a substantial raise in salary even though the program has only reached 10 per cent of the projected amount, the master of the Mint and others to explain the confusion and secrecy that has surrounded this affair from the outset-in order words, unless a complete accord accounting is made available, which I believe is only fair-we will have no alternative but to reserve our right to vote differently when the bill comes before the House for third and final reading.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) in his remarks on the bill said something that struck me as rather significant: he said that in 1976 the eyes of the world will be upon Canada. The eyes of Canada are upon Canada, and this is what really concerns me. Here we are, in this country, facing a very serious housing problem. During the last federal election I recall that when our party advocated a policy of 6 per cent mortgages, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cohorts ran around saying that that was much too rich for the people of Canada, that we could not afford it. "Where would we get money for 6 per cent mortgages?" he asked.
This Olympic thing has become a monster; it has grown out of all proportion. I remember as a child being told never to put your hat higher than you can reach it. This government has gone along with the mayor of Montreal and his grandiose ideas about how he is going to enhance Canada's image in the world by putting on one of the most spectacular performances in terms of the Olympic Games, but it smacks to me of putting one's hat higher than one can reach it economically.
It is obvious to all that we have serious priorities in this country. We have to build more houses and clean up the rivers into which we dump untreated sewage. I suggest it will be quite a scene to hold the Olympics in Montreal and to have flowing past the Olympic village in the St. Law-
June 20,1975

rence River the untreated sewage of the city. There is an unemployment rate in some parts of Quebec of 20 per cent. There is heavy unemployment in the maritimes. My colleague for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) has been harping constantly in this House since he has been here about some attention being paid to the unemployment problems of that underdeveloped and depressed area. He has pleaded with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) and the government to do something to solve those problem. Yet we are going to put on a great big spectacular, a grand circus for people who are facing very serious problems. We are going to divert their attention with a great big rah-rah-rah. We are going to tell them that even their children can become Olympic athletes. The way the tickets are selling, it is the officials and politicians who are going to get first call on the prime seats to view the Olympics.
I do not know where the priorities of this government are. I think they are sitting on their priorities. They do not even know what the Olympics in Montreal are going to cost. The Olympic committee has stated that they are going to stop publicizing the deficits because they are piling up so quickly and furiously that they cannot even keep track of them. What is it in a nation with an ego that is so big that it makes us try and outdo any other country in this kind of spectacular, at a time when we have very serious problems that need attention and the expenditure of money? I realize the federal government has stated that it is not going to finance the games beyond the provision of stamps and coins, but may I also suggest that the people of Canada are paying a very regressive kind of tax in buying lottery tickets. This kind of chance is a most regressive form of taxation and they will have to pay for it.
Over 250,000 people are going to visit the city of Montreal every day for two weeks, a city with many urban problems and transportation congestion. Oftentimes members of the House criticize the rate of violence in Montreal; it is well known and publicized every day in the newspapers. Indeed, there are criminal elements in every city. But can you imagine, Madam Speaker, 250,000 people coming together every day for two weeks and not aggravating that kind of violence? It is bad enough having General Quang there, without having an additional 250,000 visitors a day.
I know the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) is a pretty good skater, but he skated all over this issue. He could make any international skating team. I was up in the Yukon a couple of weeks ago and spent some time looking at conditions there. I must say that housing for the Indian people in the Yukon is absolutely criminal and shameful. The condition of deprivation and unhappiness that faces the native people in this country is something we can never be proud to have the eyes of the world look upon; yet the eyes of the world are upon us, and the eyes of Canada also, because of the hosting of the international games. When we are faced with dealing with the basic problems of the Canadian people, we hide behind the facade or the excuse that we cannot find the money. Yet we cannot find enough money for recreation. Let me refer to the recreation system in the riding of Nickel Belt. We have one swimming pool in the area, serving a community of 250,000 people. Half the lakes and rivers in our area have been polluted by Inco and Falconbridge who are charged with ripping out the resources of the country; yet this federal government, with its responsibility for amateur sport and recreation, cannot find the funds to build facilities for the rural communities in Canada.
This government cannot find the money to fix up the institutions where we keep those who have run afoul of the law. We keep them in buildings which are outmoded. We do not provide proper facilities to ensure the safety of

Thank you very much for reminding me, Madam Speaker. I usually get very carried away when I see waste and an irresponsible set of priorities. When the original bill was before this House to establish authority for issuing Olympic postage stamps, holding lotteries and the like, this party took the position that the priorities were all askew. We now have another bill of a similar type. Hon. friends to my right in the Progressive Conservative Party speak from both sides of their mouths. First of all they agreed there were too many anomalies in the original bill, too many unanswered questions and not a proper accounting system; yet they voted for it. Now we have Bill C-63 which will authorize the minting of Olympic gold coins. This program is supposed to raise something like $50 million, yet the last program involving the minting of silver coins fell far short of the target.
When I think of these Olympic Games and the escalation in terms of costs, I again think we have our priorities all askew. The idea of the Olympics was that people of all countries could compete in athletic events away from the politics that divide countries. When looking at Olympic schemes of today, I have to ask myself whether that idea of the Olympics is still in practice. One only has to look at the situation that surrounded the Munich Olympics to see that this has become a forum for all sorts of radical elements and a place to assassinate people. The whole concept of security is one that ought to concern us greatly, particularly when we realize that the cost of providing security will escalate just as the cost has escalated for the provision of the buildings and other facilities.
Our whole concept is wrong. Surely our concept should be one of providing proper facilities for communities in Canada so that our people can develop in a healthy way. We may well have 250,000 people watching the games and

the rest of the country participating as spectators, thanks to our television networks, the CBC being the prime agency. What we will be doing, once again, is encouraging a few select athletes to participate, with the rest of the country being spectators. Only those who have been chosen in a very contorted may will actually take part in these sports. I am sure government spokesmen will say that young people right across Canada can aspire to participation in the Olympics, but that is a concept of which I cannot conceive. In the track and field events, for example-which I know something about-one needs coaches. Surely no one believes that we are going to go out into northern Ontario and develop all kinds of athletes for the Olympics. I suggest that is a wrong concept.
We should be spending our money on providing recreational facilities in communities across Canada for the use not only of the young people but the middle-aged and the elderly, in order that all citizens can pursue physical fitness. As an example, the funds this government spends on mental health are paltry, yet mental health problems in this country will undoubtedly become even more acute. Many of our school boards do not have the kind of psychological testing services so they can identify children who may have problems at an early age. We will see more and more of the kind of thing that took place in Brampton not long ago. Alcoholism has become a very serious problem in this country, yet the funds spent by the government on alcoholic rehabilitation are paltry indeed. But we can spent millions of dollars on the glorious idea of hosting the Olympics.
One might think that the facilities that are being built for the Olympics will be available to the people of Montreal afterwards so that they can participate in amateur sports there. However, I think they will be there only for the use of professional, not amateur sports. This whole concept of developing anything for amateur sports is disgraceful. Nowhere in this country can people take part in sports for enjoyment and to compete in a friendly way one against another. Now one has to fight for something-a gold medal, a silver medal or a bronze medal: it is a highly competitive situation and the purpose is to win at all costs. Once that concept becomes embedded, there is only one way for us, and that is downward, in the philosophy of the country.
Perhaps that is what the Tories and the Liberals are interested in, to develop a competitive society: may the strong survive, and God help the weak. But that is not this party's concept. We have always been a party which has looked at the social needs and priorities. It is very obvious where the government has placed its priorities. As a matter of fact, I would like to congratulate them, but I cannot even find it in my heart to do so, over the trade mark which part of this bill will implement which shows the outline of a beaver with the Olympic symbol on its heart. It is not even an original idea. Indeed, I might even remark that the beaver shows an uncanny resemblance to the person who conceived the idea of having the Olympics in Montreal. I do not know whether it is accidental or intentional. I cannot even congratulate the government on that aspect of it.

For example, one section of the bill states that gold coins will be minted and their face value will be $100. Again, we are into that whole fuzzy area where the government brings in legislation which is unclear. As the Conservatives have pointed out, in the original bill the accounting system was unclear and the whole cost of the Olympics was up in the air. Yet they were prepared to vote for the original bill and now I suppose they will vote for this bill also. I would not be surprised at all.
This bill does not deserve to be supported. It is based on a concept that is erroneous. Indeed, if the government had courage to do what I suggest it should do, we would all be much better off. What we should be doing is letting some other country which feels it can carry the burden of the Olympics be the host for the games next summer. I do not see why the Canadian taxpayer should be burdened with that cost; and it will be a high cost. When I spoke on this bill on July 27, 1973, I predicted that the deficit would amount to $172 million. Well, that was a very conservative estimate of the loss. I suspect it will now run to $300 million or $400 million.
What are the priorities of this government? It never has money to do the things that ought to be done and to solve the problems of the people of this country. Apparently it has no mortgage money at all. The government is afraid to spend money on mortgages at 6 per cent. But we have money to throw away on the Olympics, which is a show-place and, so far as I am concerned, does not do anything for amateur sport in Canada. It may do a lot for professional sport in this country, but nothing for amateur sport.
My party does not support this bill and when the opportunity arises, if it does arise, we will vote against it because we believe it is based on the wrong concept and the wrong philosophy. When I spoke about the Olympics first, I mentioned the concept on which it should rest-a very relevant concept. I would be prepared to support a bill if it were based on such a philosophy. This bill is based on support for the Olympics in Montreal, but the Olympics are not based on the kind of philosophy I am prepared to accept.
What do we find today? The Olympic Games do not consist of the athletes of one country getting to know those of another country. The games are highly politicized. They do not leave politics off the playing field; they bring politics on to the playing field. If you read the daily reports of the Olympics you find out how many gold medals Russia or the United States have won, and how many points this or that country has won. There is a great deal of rivalry amongst the competing countries. It has many political overtones. You even hear of athletes of one country trying to entice athletes from another country to participate in games to be held in their country.

Were the government to follow the same policy, then there will be nothing left to say; were it to choose the opposite course, then Madam Speaker, beware the reaction! The Minister summarized the background of those three programs by mentioning their ups and downs.
Olympic coins did not yield the expected results because we thought we would reach a larger number of people by marketing the coins in about 55 countries of the world. As concerns stamps, I believe that

the repeated strikes have been one of the major causes of the lack of success in that area.
The minister indicated that the Olympic Lottery is a great success. I believe one of the main causes for the unprecedented success of the lottery is the publicity that has been made for years in favour of lotteries, Olympic or otherwise, or should we say invitations to participate in a risk of some sort, because Canadians love to take a chance. We should not be amazed at a deficit, considering the tremendous increase in construction costs over the last few years. There were in addition protracted strikes and salary increases that were not foreseen at the initial planning stage. We are now living in 1975 and must face up to those contingencies. Are we going to drop the Olympic Games because of such incidents? If we put the question to the workers who have been doing their part for the Olympic Games, to all the athletes that will participate, I am convinced we will get another kind of answer than the one we hear from certain speakers in this House.
As for the economics, there is a parallel with Expo 67. Because criticisms that are now levelled were heard before Expo. It was suggested that was a loss of time, of money, and so forth. But today we hear it said it was a good thing. It cost money, but it also brought revenues. We must not forget that Canadians are not the only ones to pay. Canada will get 75 per cent of the money from abroad. Yes, we will receive 75 per cent of the money from abroad. If we were to build houses, we could not count on foreign money. This in my view is one way of bringing in foreign capital. And I suggest it is economically viable.
As far as sports are concerned, I believe this is a triumph. People say nothing is done for amateur sports. I believe this will be amateur sports' triumph, if we want to further amateur sport, I think that the ideal of any amateur sportsman will be to participate in the Olympic Games. I cannot understand that any hon. member here in this House could possibly be unable to see a link between amateur sport and Olympic sport. If there is one, we must absolutely and consequently recognize the other. Now, everybody wonders "Will it be too expensive?" That is the question everybody is asking today as during Expo 67. It is too expensive, it is exaggerated, prices are too high. Today, Madam Speaker, I think we can say it is too expensive because everything is expensive. And nobody can forecast if next year we will not have 20 to 25 per cent increase.
A moment ago I heard someone who said: "I had anticipated such a year. He did not forecast anything because that sharp increase could not have been foreseen. And it is the same for all countries over the world. Our own country is not smarter than any other country. And I think that as far as forecasts are concerned today, we must bow to the facts and manage as best we can. But what is important is to achieve our objective: Canada has committed itself to host the Olympic Games and it must honour its promise lest it become the laughing stock of the world.
I think that the Olympic Games will have, at the development level, the same effect as the Montreal Expo which was the beginning of the extensive road system in Montreal. We will see such a development during and after the Olympics. It is useless to maintain that it will contribute nothing to Montreal, to Quebec and to Canada. We must not be that narrow-minded.

The representative of the Progressive Conservatives told us that the Liberals were totally inconsistent, because they were trying not to get involved in the administration of the Olympics, that they introduced a first bill promising that it would be the only support granted to the games. But today, they are presenting Bill C-63. For my part, I must congratulate the minister for introducing that bill because, having recognized that the aid was not proportionate to the efforts made by those who are now in charge, he realized that the government should give a little further assistance. I think that the bill will be welcomed by COJO.
As far as the NDP members are concerned, as we heard it a moment ago, the whole thing is too grandiose. It costs too much. Rather, we should think about housing and transportation. And yet, Madam Speaker, they are in favour of health, they say they are in favour of amateur sports; therefore, generally speaking they are in favour of sports and they continually demand more leisure. The problem should not be allowed to be displaced under the pretext that politically, it would be more valuable. We are not considering transport, health or housing, we are talking about the Olympic Games. Will they be held here? Will we be able to hold them here? Will they cost too much? We have to answer these questions.
I merely say that there must be a time for everything, but that everything must be done in its proper time. Today, we are discussing the Olympic Games; tomorrow, we will discuss transport and housing in Canada; today, however, we must consider a very urgent matter, namely whether the Olympic Games deserve the bill before us, the federal assistance which is offered today.
A moment ago, I heard the NDP member criticize the government for introducing this bill and he seemed to be saying that expenditures had not been sufficiently restricted.
Of course the government could not limit expenditures. The government is not involved in the organization, it is not involved in the administration. It provides help. The government simply donates to the Olympic Games. It is simply a donator. If the hon. member wants to criticize, he should go to the Olympic Games Organization Committee and voice his criticisms there, not to the government. When the government provides help for some deserving group, it is not involved in the administration of this group. It cannot be blamed for doing nothing about its administration. It gave its promise not to get involved in the administration and it is keeping this promise. However, at the beginning, it offered help. Could it perhaps have placed too great a limit on its promise, by saying that the only help it would provide would be the first bill on the stamps, etc.? It is the only one. It is making this new attempt because it now realizes that everything has gone up; wages have increased because of strikes, and as time goes by, it costs much, millions of dollars. The price of materials is 30, 40 or 50 per cent higher. I suppose that is why the minister is sponsoring this bill today, because as we did a year or two ago, he expected the final costs to be well established, but they exceeded all estimations. Even if the then minister had been asked to make estimations and to stick to them for five years, it would have been impossible. I shall vote for the bill.
June 20, 1975

Having considered all increases and additional administration expenses, the minister is consistent and in this bill, he will reach another part of the population. I wish him all the success he expects from this new bill, so that the province of Quebec can be told about it. In the beginning we could hear throughout the province of Quebec: "The federal is doing nothing". This afternoon, the minister gave very interesting statistics when he said that he had allocated $1 million to pay for the travels and accommodation of the athletes and $25 million for the CBC. While a budget of $56 million is forecast for the CBC, the federal government will give $25,300 million to the National Film Board. We can therefore see that finally, despite what was said at the beginning, the federal government will do something. It has already done something and it will do more, and I urge it to hold on to the end, whatever criticisms it receives, and to go on working for the honour of Canada and the welfare of Canadians.

Madam Speaker, my first words are to apologize to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) and to the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) as I missed their participation in this debate for reasons beyond my control.
I want to say that I am rising to participate as the Postmaster General whose specific role is clearly enunciated in the original bill, and that is to report to the House of Commons on certain aspects of the self-financing programs, namely, the coins and philatelic items. I enjoyed the contribution of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), as I usually do. He is always sincere, if misguided. We do not live in a fishbowl, and we do not live in isolation. It never fails to surprise me that the philosophy of the New Democratic Party is always unorthodox until it forms a government, and then it becomes very conservative. I can sum up his contribution fairly simply by saying: (a) he is against the Olympics; (b) he believes we have our priorities wrong; (c) he believes there are things to be done in the area of housing and slum clearance. Madam Speaker, very few people would disagree that there is a need for housing, slum clearance, more help for senior citizens, medicare, and so on. We all agree with this; it is a motherhood issue, in a way.
I would remind the hon. member that as on so many other occasions, the New Democratic Party seems to think it has a monopoly on this type of thinking. We all feel the same way, Madam Speaker. But life is not that simple. One does not devote all one's attention to one priority. I will not be surprised if the NDP votes against the bill. I just hope they do so from conviction and not for political expediency. If it is the latter, they might find themselves unpleasantly surprised.
In the 10 or 15 minutes toward the end of his speech, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley said that he would support the Olympics. I have become a good friend of the hon. gentleman and I know he thinks very deeply about international affairs, very deeply about the Olympics, very deeply about our country. He is one of the very few Canadians who know, from personal experience, the
Olympic Financing
cost, the effort and the time that must be devoted to becoming a perfectionist in a particular endeavour.
It is wrong for the hon. member for Nickel Belt to assume that there was ever a time in the history of the Olympics when those who rose to the top did not do so through an extraordinary dedication to their particular field of endeavour, or that there was not an aura of intense competition. We are all very competitive. The few countries where competition is not provided are very drab societies. We have many areas to improve in this country in the way of social policies but we can say that despite the imperfections it is still one of the better countries in which to live.
We have been participating in Olympic Games for the better part of a century-over 80 years. For 80 years we have had the benefit of the hospitality provided by other countries, some rich, some poor, some small and some large. Now it is our turn to host the Olympics-Canada's Olympics, not Montreal's. If there are any who oppose the Olympics going to Montreal-I hope there are not, and I know of none-I can only say that I feel sorry for people who think so narrrowly at a time this country needs to think Canada first and region second.
The hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley and the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle)-who is not a bad hockey player when he has a good defenceman backing him, as I know from personal experience-are dedicated to seeing the Olympics succeed. In recent months, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley has wanted to make sure that the games are run as efficiently as possible, that the money which has been raised for the games is accounted for as well as possible and that it is spent as efficiently as possible. He wants the Olympic Games to run smoothly and to stand for those things Canada stands for in the world.
The concept of self-financing Olympics is new. It would be wrong to create the impression that there will not be a deficit. Of course, I speak only as an individual; I have no personal knowledge of any deficit. Speaking as a member of parliament charged with a particular responsibility, I say that we should meet our commitment, which is to help the Olympic cause. We should help the Olympic committee raise a certain sum of money through COJO. It is the committee's responsibility to keeps costs in line. At no time has the federal government, as the Minister of Public Works reminded us when he spoke, committed itself either privately or openly, officially or unofficially, to assume any deficit which might or might not exist when the Olympics are over.
Having said that, I say as a Canadian and as a Montrealer that it is time to stop knocking the Olympics. This time next year we shall be on the eve of the Olympics. Let us adopt a positive attitude. If we do, the deficit could be much smaller. I think all Canadians should adopt a more positive attitude than the one displayed so far by the hon. member for Nickel Belt. If you want to be pragmatic, think of the thousands of jobs in the construction industry the games have created. The hon. member for Nickel Belt suggested that housing should be given priority. I am not arguing that his priorities are not laudable; I am simply
