speechtext:
Some people in Canada like to sit in front of a colour television set on a Saturday afternoon and watch a sports event. Their neighbours may prefer to go in the evening to Place des Arts and hear a semiamateur rendition of Faust. It all depends on what entertains you. People follow sports, amateur and professional, and they need not apologize because that happens to be their chosen form of recreation, their chosen form of escape from the problems of an ever more complex world.
In this bill we ask for little. It is apparent that we are committed to the raising of a sum of money which was determined several years ago when I was not a member of the cabinet but a member of this House. We are asking for the right to deviate from the provisions of the original bill to the extent that we want to mint a gold coin. But we do not ask the House for any right to raise the total face value of the $450 million worth of silver and gold coins which are to be minted; nor are we asking to increase the $250 million figure, the figure which would have been reached if certain events had not taken place and which, hopefully, may still be reached. This money would be turned over to the committee for the financing of the Olympics. I was pleased to note that the Minister of Public Works indicated in his contribution to the debate that we intend to help the financing of the Commonwealth Games to be held in Edmonton in 1978, with a similar program.
Sports, at least in the province I come from, are more important than almost anything else, including education, in bringing together the various elements of society. When the hon. member for Joliette and the hon. member for Verdun are playing on a team, they forget very quickly that their only difference is that of language. When you are playing hockey or any other sport, professionally or as an amateur, you are not worried whether the person on your left is English, French or of any other ethnic background, provided he protects your blind side when you look the other way.
There has been a tremendous spin-off from the Olympics. I don't know about anybody else, but when I wander around at eight o'clock in the morning I am almost knocked down by civil servants jogging on the streets. I do not know what they are running from: I know it is not from their minister, or to him. Perhaps they are following some Treasury Board directive. In all seriousness, we are learning what other countries have known for centuries that your mental and physical processes work better when you are fit. Physical fitness is becoming one of our priorities in Canada. I think the Olympics have contributed to this spirit.
Last night a Canadian editorial writer said that it is time Canadians stopped knocking the Olympics in Montreal; it is time they stopped being negative about the deficit. I agree. The games will be one of the wonders of the world. They will be as successful as we can possibly make them, and already we have learned an awful lot. For instance, Olympics will no longer be awarded to cities, but to countries: although the games were awarded to Mont-

real, they will in future be awarded to a country. This will go a long way toward meeting objections raised by hon. gentlemen and others. The games will be more highly decentralized and we can reduce cost pressures on an individual region, costs which have prevented many Third World countries from participating as hosts.
Hosting the Olympic Games is no easy task. When you think about them you must pause, reflect, approve, innovate-then return to reality. No doubt in many ways the Olympics have become overcommercialized; perhaps the underlying theme is no longer that of brotherhood. But the answer is not to destroy the Olympics, not to destroy an institution of society and then think about replacing it; the answer is to reform it from within. This process is going on as a result of the lessons we have learned.
Whether you like it or not, this first experience in self-financing has been remarkably successful, if you consider how much it was estimated would need to be raised and what has been raised. The three programs which the House permitted, those involving stamps, coins and lotteries, have been successful. The target of $290 million will be reached. The lottery has actually exceeded expectations. While the coins have not reached their potential, the lottery has exceeded its potential. On the philatelic side, it will probably be on target. If there is a deficit, it will not be because we did not raise the sums of money needed but because of escalating costs associated with the Olympics.
In all fairness to Mayor Drapeau and CO JO, I do not know of anything today that has not escalated out of sight. Every country in the world is faced with the problem of inflation. It would be rather naive to think that a project as big as the Olympics, physically and in every other way, would not also be subject to inflation that was unpredictable when the concept of bringing the Olympics to Canada was thought of several years ago. We have to be fair. I understand that labour costs, salary costs, promotion and all the rest have escalated. I do not know whether there is waste or to what degree there is waste. I do know that inflation has reared its ugly head internationally. I know it has had a detrimental effect on the over-all cost of the Olympics. However, it seems we have spent a lot of time on the deficit, to the detriment of the Olympics Games themselves.
The Olympics will take place in 13 months whether we like it or not. As Canadians, we must either develop a positive attitude or continue in a negative spirit. I happen to believe that they will be a success, not simply for Montreal but for this country. I gauge that by the interest in amateur sport across the country and the interest in Olympic tickets. Ticket offices have been flooded for requests from one end of Canada to the other.
I want to speak for a few minutes about the coin program and the philatelic side of the operation. I say in all sincerity to the member opposite that the questions he asked are pertinent, positive and deserve an answer to the degree to which we are capable of doing so during the committee hearings. I must come back to the point made by the Minister of Public Works, namely, that we have limited responsibility at the federal level. From the very beginning we limited to the greatest possible degree any
June 20, 1975

commitment to participate in the deficit. For that particular reason we have stayed, I will say, at arm's length; we have asked; we have checked.
I will be appearing before the committee. I am certain that any questions asked about my area of responsibility- which is a direct one; coins and stamps-will be answered with conviction and truth. If I cannot answer, I can guarantee this House that some official will. If he does not answer honestly and sincerely, he will be on unemployment insurance the next day. That is the best I can promise.
I know the hon. member did not intend this, but if we are to use the committee as a witch hunt, spending several weeks unintentionally developing a negative attitude to the Olympics, we will once again contribute to the deficit. Every time there have been problems, work stoppages, construction stoppages, material shortages, concerns with meeting IOC the date, inquiries in Europe by the IOC, this group or that group, or there has been any other uncertainty concerning the Olympics, there has been a direct negative effect on our program. I can show that by the graphs put together indicating the uncertainty and the sales.
If in committee we can once and for all get rid of the negative attitude in this country and get behind the program, we will go a long way toward meeting these abnormally high costs of the Olympics and making a success of our program. It needs a positive approach from all Canadians. I say "all" Canadians because we as politicians often get out of touch. There is a greater acceptance of the Olympics outside the House of Commons than inside, as the official spokesman for the New Democratic Party made very clear.
I am going to touch on some times that I think the hon. member and others would like to know about, without, of course, intending to go into committee of the whole at the moment. I must take slight exception to one remark made by the hon. member: it was about the competence of Mr. Page, and his salary. There was an inference that the coin program is not a success. I think we are very fortunate in our choice of Mr. Page. This is the first time in our history that we have tried to raise money in this way. It is very hard to gauge success since there is nothing to gauge it against. However, it is significant that we had to begin at day one on a successful level. We have not had the same opportunity as private enterprise with one, two or three years of deficits in order to build up the operation. We have needed to have success from the beginning.
There have been a lot of abnormal, unforeseen events which have affected the silver coins program. Nevertheless, I am convinced we will surpass the realistic target of $100 million. My appraisal of what has been going on, from very detailed questioning over the past week, indicates that we will reach or surpass the $100 million in the silver coins program. At no time did we suggest $250 million. The bill states that in the event the program "takes off," we are not to turn over more than $250 million. It is fortunate that we did not put a ceiling of $32 million on the lottery. It is bringing in hundreds of millions of dollars. The three programs, together, which this parliament permitted the organization to adopt will, in the final analysis, reach the total that we set out to meet.

I hope the hon. member is not bringing in the concept that we should be paid according to our value, because there are 265 salaries in the House of Commons and a lot of members are underpaid and a lot are overpaid. If Mr. Page had taken the job on a percentage basis, he would be making a lot more money than at present, because it has netted COJO over $100 million in the short time he has been in charge of the program. I suggest, as we have had an increase in pay, that he should be the last to make any inference about Mr. Page's increased remuneration. We suggested profits to COJO of $100 million. We will, I think-I say "I think" because I cannot promise it-surpass that amount.
We were authorized to mint not more than $450 million in coin and we will stay within that boundary, including the gold program. We are presently selling the silver coins in 75 countries around the world. We have had to do this beginning within six months of the passage of the original legislation. We sold in the first year close to $100 million worth and grossed about 30 per cent, which is good for any business starting out; I do not know too many companies in Canada which have been able to match that. We have paid our own costs, and not a single penny of taxpayers' money has been used in the program. The expenses have been taken from the gross.
The program which Mr. Page supervises employs 500 people directly or indirectly in manufacturing the coins, packaging, supplying, marketing, and distributing to over 1,500 Canadians at the moment. We contributed $40 million last year to Canada's balance of trade and we have, I believe, made a lot of new friends and customers for Canada around the world.
As the hon. member knows, there have been events- and I do not wish to gloss them over-which have affected sales beyond the first series. Not least, of course, has been the tremendous increase in the cost of raw material-in this case, silver. We had a difficult decision to make. Should we make the coins smaller, should we debase the currency, should we reduce the silver content? We refused to do it. We were producing coins of sterling silver and we still are, coins of the same dimension and of the same high quality, in line, I think, with our responsibility to the Canadian people. Even though to decrease the value of the coins would be to increase the potential profit, I believe the decision taken was a wise one in the light of our high reputation in the coin markets around the world.
We ran into a general recession in some countries, depression in others. Official government policy in Japan negated sales there and, for a while, as the hon. member

June 20, 1975

knows, there was difficulty in penetrating the U.S. market. In the year I have been around I think I have done a few things to help Mr. Page rectify the weaknesses in some of these areas.
We are now working very closely with the banks. Some of the chartered banks could have helped a little more than they did. They now seem to be giving us the type of support which I believe the banks in this country ought to be giving us in view of the privileged position they enjoy in our business community. The regional meetings we are holding with senior bank officials have resulted in new pledges that we would receive much greater support from here onward.
We have started a direct mailing campaign. Through Chargex and Master Charge we are soliciting clients among six million potential customers. We are now engaged on the second wave of direct mail credit cards issued by the oil companies. Here is another mailing list of ten million names. Robert Simpson and Woodwards have been kind enough to place our pamphlets on their subscription lists and this will enable us to reach another 1.2 million subscribers. Simpsons-Sears have already participated through their stores; they have been good corporate citizens, particularly in Toronto. I am pleased with the help given by Mr. Burton, and from our conversation I think they will go even further in the future. We are discussing the program with other large companies such as Eatons and the Bay.
Pay-roll deduction arrangements are already in place with Air Canada. We are negotiating with Canada Steamships and Imperial Oil. The response from Air Canada has been remarkably encouraging; many employees have taken advantage of the pay-roll deduction scheme to buy coins, including the back issue. Of course the coin dealers are participating but, as the hon. member knows, business in this sector fluctuates depending upon whether the dealers are speculating or whether they are dealing in a more traditional manner.
Without boring the House with too many of the details I can discuss later in the committee, may I say that in addition to this we are touring 30 Canadian cities with our art display. We have turned over hundreds of thousands of dollars directly for the benefit of amateur sport in this country and the training of athletes.
As to the operation in the United States, we are working directly with American Express, and through their direct mail service we have sold 40,000 subscriptions in the last two months. We are still getting many calls for the first set. So I would say the American market is finally being penetrated. Shell, Penney's, Gimble's, Macy's are all participating. There seems to be a more positive attitude, less resistance to and more awareness of the beauty of Canadian coins.
Europe has been our best market, our most stable market, because collecting is traditional there. It is a form of hedging and we are aware of it. We are doing our best to expand that market even further. In the far Pacific we are dealing through 500 various banks and we are finally penetrating the Japanese market through the credit card system.

Finally, may I say we are working extremely hard to promote the silver coin program in this country, and I believe events will prove that Canadians are accepting these silver coins in very large numbers.
This brings me to the subject of the gold coins. We have a standard of excellence in this country in our coin program and one which we do not intend to debase even for the Olympics. Our gold coins must contain sufficient gold as not to make a mockery of gold coinage. Yet we must be realistic; we cannot simply turn over $100 worth of gold dust for a $100 bill. We have to hit a happy medium and produce a result which will appeal to the traditional speculator in Europe as well as to Canadians who are less concerned about the value of the coin as measured by the amount of gold it contains, but who give more consideration to the fact that it is money of the realm and can be used as such at any time.

The hon. member asks how much. Well, we shall be producing the gold coins in two qualities to sell for two prices. I am talking because I am not sure how much gold they will contain. I am looking. We measure gold a little differently from silver. The expression used is "fine gold". I would say there would be at least a quarter of an ounce in one and at least half an ounce in the other. In other words, we would have a coin for the numismatic market, polished and so on-all the things collectors appreciate-and the other would be more of a circulating coin, a coin which would be sold by the banks for $100 plus a small premium. So we are asking Canadians to invest $100 in paper money for a $100 gold coin plus a small premium. And I think people will accept it.
We must not forget, though, that we have a responsibility to coin collectors not to flood the market with gold coins. So again we have a problem deciding how many will be minted. This is being worked out, and it is one of the questions I can answer during the committee stage.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, may I say that I think the contribution of the hon. member for High Park-Humb-er Valley in recent months, and the contribution of the hon. member for Nickel Belt, who sometimes gets under our skin because he reminds us periodically that there are certain values of life that we tend to forget now and then, have been positive ones. The time has come to think positively about the Olympics, and I will do my best to help establish that mood by being as forthright as possible with hon. members when we get to committee stage.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am certainly very happy to take part in the debate this afternoon on this bill which aims at ensuring the success of the 1976 Olympics.
I listened very attentively to my colleague from High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek), and I know that the government members also listened with interest to his observations, which I found quite relevant in view of the importance of the credits voted to these games. I therefore think that if it is normal that we should pass legislation to
June 20, 1975

finance the games, it is also normal that we should demand to know what is going on and what use is made of these funds.
I am very pleased with the remarks of my hon. colleague and the speech of the Postmaster General who, all in all, has invited us to adopt a positive attitude towards the Olympic Games. I feel he was right in urging hon. members to adopt an objective, positive and fair attitude in that matter. On this basis, there will be a number of questions to be asked in committee, and they will be asked objectively, so that the Canadian public may understand better how the money is being spent and the reasons why costs are rising so rapidly.
As many of my colleagues, I have noticed that the hon. member reminded the government of its priorities. I feel that his comparisons were somewhat questionable and irrelevant. It is clear that a government must have priorities. I think that physical fitness and motivation through the Olympic Games should be one of the government's priorities. I am very happy that mention was made of the diversification or decentralization of the various sports. My colleague, on my right, would like to see a certain amount of decentralization. I agree; the idea is very sensible; my only regret is that the idea was not discussed when Canada submitted its application for the Olympic Games to be held in Montreal.
In any event, there is some decentralization in my area, since the archery contests will be held in the beautiful city of Joliette. And of course I rejoice that my riding should be so honoured. Mr. Speaker, the Olympic Act, which was passed almost three years ago, was meant to meet the needs at the time. Optimism ran high with regard to the act and the financial resources which were expected to be adequate. So, maybe we could ask this question. What happened since, in view of the fact that the Minister deems it necessary to introduce a new legislation, which we will support without any hesitation? I was quite eager to support the first bill, and I would also like to understand first the reasons underlying the presentation of a second one. Of course, we could dwell a long time on inflation, which caused some difficulties, particularly strikes. I think there are things people do not think about, and these are the requirements of the International Committee concerning facilities.
I know the International Committee is very demanding. Would it not be appropriate to urge those responsible for the Olympics at an international level to be more serious and practical when speaking about facilities and services we want to provide to athletes and which athletes require themselves? I know from a most reliable source that COJO has the problem of answering very costly requests, and of course initial estimates have been exceeded. By how much? Both sides were shocked by the additional costs. I would like nevertheless to put a couple of questions to the hon. members, since I think it is important today to appeal to the understanding of the hon. members on the issue of additional costs. We have a right to ask COJO officials to explain the reasons for these increases. For the National Art Centre in Ottawa, I think that the final cost was six or seven times higher than the initial estimate and the climate was far better; there was no inflation. We had no difficulties in the building industry. I
Olympic Financing
feel that we could think of other people who also committed errors before thinking of those who evaluated the cost of the Olympic Games. I do not remember the initial cost of the Mirabel Airport and I still do not know how much it will cost. When such evaluations or comparisons will have been made, I think that we may be in a better position to understand the situation and that COJO administrators will have achieved greater success than those who were in charge of both these projects.
Not so long ago the government seemed to want to refuse any additional aid. It gave us the impression that it was trying to stay clear of the problem because several people and organizations were criticizing these additional costs. At the time I regretted the government's intention to stay clear. The idea of supporting in principle as well as in fact the project of holding the Olympic Games in Canada in 1976-had been accepted by the government, and I think that we must now appeal for the open support of each and every Canadian. I feel it is our responsibility, as Canadians and as members of this House, to provide for and facilitate the financing of these games. I deem it unthinkable for us to try and stay clear of the project.
The government introduced today a bill that will hopefully provide for the financing of the games. I listened with much interest to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) when he referred to the great number of services now offered for the games. I know this will involve many thousands of dollars, in addition to this new formula for financing COJO's administration. I am very interested in and I appreciate the efforts to help in the achievement and success of the Olympic Games. I feel that, as members of this House, we must objectively try to provide for easier and more numerous services on the occasion of that event.
Some measures were announced for athletes in particular, and it must be remembered that this participation is at the national level. What did we do, for instance, to prepare our athletes for competition? This is a highly pertinent question. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who his responsible for amateur sport, has indicated for a few years that more money will be voted. Mr. Speaker, I would just like to put a few remarks on the record about this bill. I took part in the debate the last time and, as I recall, I was the last speaker before the measure was passed. As the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) has said, we support the principle and the spirit of the Olympic Games. I do not think there is anything we want to see more than the success of the Olympic Games in Montreal. Whether there is a deficit or not is something else again, but certainly we want to see the games go ahead and succeed.
I think we all shared the feelings of many Candians a few weeks ago when there was some doubt about whether the games would go ahead. I was sorry for the people at COJO because of the events that have taken place in Montreal in the last few months. These people are not responsible for the strikes, the disruptions, the police commission report, or any of those things which cast a cloud or a pall over the Olympic committee's efforts. We support the principle and the concept of the Olympic Games and we want them to be a great success. I know they will be, and that Candians generally will be very proud of our contribution to the Olympics.
I was rather surprised by some of the remarks of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). It seems to me that in the last few weeks I have spoken following that hon. member, so I have had the opportunity of taking a few shots at him, as he does at us when he has the opportunity. I was more than surprised when the hon. member said that in his view the Olympic Games would not do anything for the mental or physical health of the children of this country. That is a very surprising statement in view of my own experience, which I should like to relate to the House to illustrate what the Olympic Games mean to me as an individual.
When I was seven years old I had polio. I was cripped, wore braces, and used crutches. This is an experience that not very many people have had. When I was in bed recovering from this illness I used to dream about the Olympics. One of the great athletes of that day was Glen Cunningham, whom I am sure the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) remembers. He had been caught in a fire, his legs were badly burned, and he was crippled. I remember my mother reading me a story about Glen Cunningham and how hard he worked to recover.
After several years of determination, exercise, falling down, being bruised, cut, and exhausted, I learned to walk again. Then, after a few years, I learned to run again.

We found that the coins were designated as the legal tender of Canada, and then further on in the bill we found that the minister would be authorized to sell the coins at a discount. To those of us who have had any experience in commerce it was incomprehensible that we should be selling our legal tender at a discount. We had one memorable meeting with the postmaster general of the day, now the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), who will remember that meeting because it went on until two o'clock in the morning. At that meeting we found out that there was a Swiss bank which was going to buy $100 million worth of Olympic coins. It was incredible that we, as members, could not learn from the two ministers present at the meeting the name of the Swiss bank. We were told it was confidential information, information which was given to COJO.
I was a new member at the time and I thought pretty highly of the standing of members of parliament. It was incredible to me that we would be sitting at a meeting with two ministers of the Crown and would be denied the name of a bank that was negotiating to buy $100 million worth of coins. It was confidential information. Every secretary in COJO knew about it, but members of parliament who were going to pass legislation to bring this coin bill into effect were denied this information.
Of course we found out the name of the bank. It was well known in banking circles. It turned out that it was not really a bank at all, it was a couple of fellows dealing in foreign exchange. It was not a bona fide bank.

He said: Mr. Speaker, my motion is that Bill S-24, an act to incorporate the Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
The bill is in standard form as prescribed by the Bank Act, and was amended in the Senate to change the name from the National Commercial Bank of Canada, to remove the word national which had been opposed by certain other financial institutions.
The sponsors of the proposed bank are Boyd, Stott and McDonald Limited, a reputable financial institution which has had considerable experience in the Canadian financial markets, with an acute awareness of the role of the banks, insurance, loan and trust companies that operate in them.
A group of six eminent and responsible Canadians are represented as provisional directors, who will, if this bill is given second reading, attend the meeting of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
Without taking an undue amount of the time of the House, I would like briefly to discuss the present position of the banking situation in Canada.
As all hon. members are aware, the banking industry in Canada is dominated by large, successful banks, with a total system encompassing some 7,000 branches. The service provided by this system assures most people in

Canada of ready access to banking facilities. As Canada grows so does its banking system. As a consequence it is now evident that there is room for specialization in banking to supplement the present system. Evidence of this is provided by the recent growth of foreign banks doing a specialized commercial business.
The principal concept behind the Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank is that it is to be a business oriented bank as distinct from a full service bank. Instead of a large multibranch system, there would be a few branches, each of which would be located in a key commercial centre of Canada.
The management of this bank would be specialized in a manner that would be responsive to local needs.
The lending policy would be of a specialized character and would be principally oriented to small business loans and commercial loans in such areas as construction and bridge financing new ventures or resource financing.
Deposits would be acquired in money markets rather than from consumer deposits.
The capitalization of the Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank as provided in Bill S-24 will be $40 million of $10 par value shares. It is planned by the sponsors to obtain an initial subscription of $22 million.
The initial offer to subscribe will be made to Canadian financial institutions, primarily trusteed pension funds.
A feature of considerable importance is that the head office of the bank will be located in the city of Vancouver. As one of the fastest growing metropolitan areas in North America and Canada's third largest city it is believed by the sponsors to be an ideal location.
There undoubtedly will be a number of questions which hon. members will wish to ask prior to the passage of the bill. It is hoped that before third reading is given to this bill the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs will provide a full opportunity for such examination.

speechtext:
As a member of my party's finance committee and a member representing a Vancouver constituency, and Vancouver is where the head office of the Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank will be, I have a particular interest in this bill. However, I also feel compelled to be somewhat critical of the federal government for its past actions or lack of action in the banking field. The west has been ignored by the federal government on many scores, not the least important of which is banking.
Not too many years ago applications for the incorporation of two banks which would have centred their opera-
June 20, 1975

tions in western Canada were rejected. A few years ago, when the provincial government of British Columbia wanted to own a minority interest in the proposed Bank of British Columbia in order to ensure its safe and early birth, permission was refused. Despite that, the Bank of Columbia was launched with the moral support of the British Columbia government; it is thriving and serving well the needs of British Columbians.
That was not good enough for our new premier who, just one month ago, announced the creation of a new financial institution to serve the financial needs of the citizens of B.C. Being unable to invest in or create a bank, British Columbia will form the British Columbia Savings and Trust which, says the premier, will give the people of B.C. a real alternative to the traditional types of financial institutions.
What has the federal government done? Last fall, in response to pressures from many quarters, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduced Bill C-7, which received first reading on October 3 of last year. This bill has the dual purpose of enabling banks to be incorporated by the ordinary letters patent method rather than by special act of parliament, and of enabling a provincial government to own up to 10 per cent of the stock in a bank. That is a fine move, you may say, and without binding in any way my party to the support of Bill C-7, I would say that I agree. My party has not made a decision on Bill C-7 because, as everyone in this House knows, only items which the government brings forward for debate can be considered. Until the government presents Bill C-7 for second reading, to be followed by committee consideration, the stale old procedures must be followed. Keeping a bill on the order paper for eight months is no way to improve the banking system.
The government's inaction is what has brought on today's debate. One may be inclined to think that there are too many banks; but one must look at the areas which are being well served, and then at those which are being badly served. Until recently head office-which means eastern head office-approval was required for relatively small business loans to Vancouver businesses. Legal limits have been increased, but the total availability of credit is still subordinated to eastern needs.
The proposed Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank is backed by an extremely active and obviously capable group. This group's credits include the Mortgage Insurance Corporation of Canada, which was incorporated by act of parliament in 1963 and which complements the insuring of mortgages by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This company permitted the creation of high ratio insured loans and has largely eliminated the old style high discount, high cost second mortgage.
This group which is proposing the establishment of the new bank has also been responsible for the uncovering of large pools of capital for use in the west. This has been done through the Morguard Trust Company and its parent, Morguard Investment Services Ltd., which was founded in 1966. Since then the company has invested two thirds of its funds, or some $400 million, in mortgages in western Canada, and nearly $200 million in mortgage funds has been raised in western Canada.
Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank
Now these perceptive gentlemen have found a further need, which they intend to meet. The new Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank will be a businessman's bank, and my colleague from Mississauga outlined in some detail some of its proposed operations. We ought to take note that it will be owned by businessmen, operated by businessmen, and will be doing business with businessmen. The managers of the large pension funds, and other funds are looking for an investment like the Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank into which they can place their funds with confidence. It is not the intention of the promoters, if I may use that term in the businessman's sense, to seek out the average, individual investor, and the stock of this new bank will not be listed on any stock exchange.
Managers of local businesses in the west are looking for a business oriented bank to fulfill their needs. As I pointed out, in some cases businessmen in the west have found it difficult to obtain loans simply because the large banks are eastern oriented.
The new bank will be operating in the relatively sophisticated money markets, but will not need to tread with the extreme caution with which the deposit oriented banks must tread. I submit that the bank will be better able to accommodate businessmen in their operations. It will also be of continuing benefit to the ordinary businessman who needs temporary, extra capital quickly with the local approval that this new bank will be able to give.
For all these reasons, and for others which may come forward, I am hopeful of the support of all members so that this bill can be considered by the standing committee.

Mr. Speaker, normally I see little merit in creating additional chartered banks in this country, as over the years it has become obvious that chartered banks are not prepared to take some of the risks which must be taken in an innovative society. Therefore we need people to enter the banking field who are prepared to take greater risks than chartered banks are normally prepared to take, and to lend money to businessmen under conditions which ordinary chartered banks would not accept. For that reason I support this bill on second reading and say that it ought to be sent to committee where important questions can be raised.
Having heard the previous speaker say that we need local banking institutions in the west I hope, if and when the government of British Columbia comes before this House and proposes the establishment of a bank to be incorporated by the government of British Columbia, that proposal will meet as much sympathy and understanding as the proposal now before the House has met.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TWO MORE GENERAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY
speechtext:
that Bill C-249, to amend the Canada Labour Code (provision for ten general holidays with pay), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a bill that has been around for a number of years in one form or another. The House seems to be in a congenial mood this afternoon. It has already passed one bill and sent it to committee. There have been other expressions of good will. One can always hope that this bill might at least be sent to committee by five o'clock today.

The purpose of this bill is to add two holidays to the list of holidays included in the Canada Labour Code. Perhaps at this point I might indicate that the legislation respecting holidays in Canada is somewhat mixed up. First, there are holidays under federal jurisdiction and holidays under provincial jurisdiction. There are holidays that are simply declared by law to be holidays and that is all there is to it. But in the case of the Canada Labour Code there is a provision that certain days be listed as holidays and that people get those days off without loss of pay. There is also a provision about extra time that workers will be paid if they are required to work on those days. It is that law, the Canada Labour Code, which I am seeking to amend by this bill this afternoon.
I again make the point that in so far as federal jurisdiction is concerned we can deal with labour matters for about only 10 per cent of the working population. The other 90 per cent of the workers in this country come under provincial labour jurisdiction. The dividing line is set out in a rather lengthy portion of the British North America Act.
If I may capsulize it a bit, the general rule is that persons employed in industries like railways, steamships, communications, banks and so on, those businesses that are clearly nation-wide and clearly cross provincial boundaries, come under federal labour jurisdiction. Therefore the holiday arrangements for railway workers, bank clerks, and some of these other groups come under federal law.
Each province makes its own law regarding holidays and whether workers will get extra pay if they have to work on those holidays. However, there is a fairly general rule that the provincial laws are pretty close to the federal law. In some instances the provinces get ahead of the federal. In other instances, the federal leads the way.
I make these few introductory remarks, not in the hope that by passing this bill it will settle the question of holidays for all workers in Canada, but that it will help to set the pattern. If we can get to the point where we have ten days in the year that are holidays, in the sense that the workers get extra pay if they have to work and do not lose pay for not working, for the 10 per cent who come under federal labour jurisdiction, it will not be long until we have the same provisions under the provincial laws across this country.
I would like to say a word or two about the history of this bill. When the present labour code was brought in so far as holidays are concerned, the then Minister of Labour, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), had in it a provision for seven general holidays. That is what they are called in this legislation. In other words, there were seven days workers would get off without loss of pay, or for which they would get double or triple time if they had to work.
When that bill was going through the House, actually in committee of the whole, we were able to get added to that number one more holiday, namely, Remembrance Day. That is the law at the present time. There are eight general holidays in the Canada Labour Code. Thus there are eight days that workers must get off without loss of pay or, if they have to work, they get overtime rates of pay.
June 20, 1975

I should like to read the list of those days. They are days that everyone would guess. Before I do so, I should like to point out that in the law as it now stands there is authority to substitute a different day for any one of these. For example, in the province of Quebec, St. Jean Baptiste Day can be substituted for one of the others and so on. Those days actually named in the Canada Labour Code are New Year's Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, as it is called in the law, July 1, Labour Day, Thanksgiving, Remembrance Day and Christmas.
Shortly after we got this list of eight general holidays set out in the law, I started bringing in a bill to add one more, a ninth day. The day that I proposed was a day the equivalent of the civic holiday that is observed in most parts of Canada on the first Monday in August. I remember well some of the debates that took place on that bill. In fact one member across the way, who used to take part more often in private members' hour debates than he does now, took part in it.
When I was asking that the ninth holiday be in August, ski enthusiasts said why not make it in February. I remember saying that if it were in February, others would say why not make it in August. Some wanted it in August. Some wanted it in February. The compromise was simple. When I brought in the bill the next year I put them both in, a day in August and a day in February.
There were also arguments about what to call the day. We on the opposition side run into this all the time. It does not matter how good a suggestion we make, from the benches across the way there has to be some criticism of it or some other suggestion to make. I decided I would meet that by drawing my bill in such a way that it would provide for an additional holiday in August and an additional holiday in February without, so far as the bill is concerned, either naming the precise dates or giving names to the holidays. I suggest that could be arrived at in either one of two ways. It could be done either by proclamation or it could be done by the committee to which the bill may be referred. In other words, my desire is to get a February holiday and an August holiday for those workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction whatever the precise dates or whatever names might be attached to those days.

So, Mr. Speaker, for a number of years now I have been calling for these two additional days. In the meantime others have proposed various February holiday. One former colleague of mine had one; the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) has a proposal for a holiday to celebrate the birthday of the first prime minister of this country. There were several other bills-Heritage Day, Flag Day, and so on.
Several of those bills got referred to the appropriate standing committee a year or two ago, and out of that standing committee came a compromise or a consensus, which was to the effect that there should be a day in February and that it should be called Heritage Day. Well, it almost got through in the last parliament but it did not quite make the grade. The committee made a repbrt to that effect, and we were on the way, but we never got there. In this parliament the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville
Canada Labour Code
(Mr. MacGuigan) took it upon himself to put in a private member's bill, C-208, which if I am correct spells out precisely what the committee in the last parliament recommended, and he therefore proposed that there be a holiday in February to be known as Heritage Day.
I think it is a piece of irony that his bill, C-208, has got along fairly well. It has received second reading, it has been through the standing committee and it has been reported. It has gone through the report stage and all that is required now is third reading, but for some reason or other the hon. member does not seem to wish to move the third reading motion.
On the sheet of paper which is sent around and which tells one what is scheduled for private members' hour, I find his name. Today he is to respond to my second reading motion on Bill C-249. I am not suggesting there is a conflict of interest and that he is going to oppose my bill just because he wants his. If he would move third reading of his bill-C-208-and there was a chance of getting it through, I would sit down right now and let him do it. I do not detect any offer, though. He does not stand.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I hope it will make the point I want to put to the House that I think it would not be unreasonable for me to ask for my bill, or the subject matter thereof, to be sent to the committee so there can be further discussion about this whole question. If I am told that the only difference between my bill and the bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville is that his calls for a holiday in February and mine calls for a holiday in both February and August, I would point out that it is not the only difference.
The bill of the hon. member merely declares Heritage Day to be a holiday. There would be some proclamations, and fine speeches, and patriotic utterances and so on. But there is no provision for pay for the day being taken off as a holiday; it does not provide for any overtime pay for those who have to work on that day. That is the difference.
My bill not only provides for a February and August holiday instead of just one, but it provides that those days be listed in the Canada Labour Code and therefore get the benefit of holiday provisions under that law. That is why, since the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville does not seem to be proceeding, as much as I wish he would, with his Bill C-208, I should like to see my bill go to committee so there could be discussion of two points-one, that we add another day to the list, and two, that we put them in a category that will provide for the day off with pay for the workers of this country, and for overtime pay for those who have to work.
That is the situation, Mr. Speaker. Some may say that an August holiday is enjoyed by many Canadians already and ask why we should put it into the code. Well, it is not there now and therefore it does not become a holiday with pay for railway workers and others covered under the Code. It is a holiday only in those cities where the civic administration declares it to be a holiday. Whether or not workers get the holiday depends, of course, upon their collective agreements or the arrangements between employers and employees. It is only when you get holidays listed firmly in a code, such as the eight I have named which are in the federal code and the holidays which are listed in the provincial labour codes, that you get holidays

June 20, 1975
Canada Labour Code
which are holidays in the full sense, so that workers get paid when they do not work on those days. I think there is definite room for improvement in this situation.
I heard some cracks around when I said I had a bill to present today. I was asked what it was I was trying to abolish. Well, I am not trying to abolish anything. I am trying to establish something, namely, that there be at least ten paid holidays in the Canada Labour Code for the workers who come under that legislation, and that in so doing we lay down a pattern which I hope may be followed by the provinces.
I have the feeling, Mr. Speaker, that there is nobody in the House of Commons who disagrees with this idea of increasing the number of holidays. I have the feeling there is nobody who disagrees with the idea that if we are going to provide holidays then our workers should get paid for them. I know the chances of the bill getting passed and on down the road in this last half hour of Friday afternoon, are not as good as they might be. But certainly the matter could be given the further study which goes with the bill itself or its subject matter being sent to the appropriate standing committee.
This is one more chapter in the long battle for sufficient numbers of holidays with pay. I think having one in August for sure is a good idea. I think having one in February for sure, to break that long spell between Christmas and Good Friday, is a good idea, and I hope that one way or another the House will show its support this afternoon and agree to send the bill or even its subject matter to the appropriate standing committee.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TWO MORE GENERAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), whose time in this House has been marked by a continued desire to improve the lot of Canadians who might be considered disadvantaged. I think he takes second place to no one with respect to that.
I am one of those who share the view that it is not necessarily wrong that there be a couple of extra holidays in a year-with pay, as he said-and with whatever would be deemed reasonable in terms of extra compensation for those who would have to work on those days. In an age when our society is becoming complex, when many of the industrial functions are becoming routine and boring, and some of them, I am told by some people on assembly lines, are becoming mind destroying, there is some advantage to that kind of thing.
I want to say something with respect to a different form of holiday that we might consider in the course of considering this bill when it ever gets to a committee, or the subject matter gets to a committee, and that is what is really behind that word holiday. I don't mean this necessarily in the theological sense, but a holiday can have a religious connotation. It can have a national connotation. It is a day of celebration in some way. It is not just a day of recreation.
If we are to establish a day, whether in February or August, we should think of it as a celebration by Canadians who live in a country that is rich when compared with

other nations of the world, not just in the monetary sense but in terms of the advantages inherited by its citizens. I speak of the democratic way of life, the importance of institutions, the right of dissent-all those things important to people living in society, things that are denied other people in many other countries of the world. In fact, we are a minority among nations.
If we look upon a holiday in that sense, we should dedicate it to a celebration of the richness that we enjoy in this country by giving something back to the country in a voluntary way. We give something to our country in terms of our taxation. We give something to our country in terms of the work we do as Canadians. We give something to our country every day we become involved in community activity. But these contributions tend to be isolated instances; in the national sense there is no co-ordination with respect to them. Therefore a lot of the things that could be done, that are attempted in a hit and miss fahion, could be co-ordinated in a national day of celebration.
I hope that in considering this bill one of these days can be set aside as a national community development days, a day when we give something ourselves in the voluntary sense in developing our communities. I suppose we are concerned about the fact that our society is becoming a less desirable place to live as we pack more and more people into fewer and fewer acres of land. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) says he is fighting the problems of our cities, and so he should be.
We are polluting our air with our waste, in the same way as we are polluting our waters. We denude the country of trees. Perhaps for one such day we might consider something like an arbor day when each of us would resolve that somewhere in this country we would plant a tree, or we would take part in cleaning up a piece of public property for nothing, or we would engage in projects to clean up the rivers, creeks, and other bodies of water in our area, in an organized way. We could also remember the tremendous disadvantages faced by some of our citizens, the retarded children of this country who need our attention the most and get it the least.
In that sense I look upon this not as a day of rest necessarily but as a day of voluntary work, a day of commitment. For those who cannot partake in that day of commitment in a voluntary way, perhaps we should each make a contribution from our salary or wages to a charity or some organization for the public good in our community. That would be a real celebration of the fortunate situation we enjoy in this country. The organizations to which I am referring were not established to assist the advantaged, the fortunate; they were established to assist the unfortunate. Those who have the ability and good fortune to work could perhaps make that kind of contribution. Others, young and old, could make a contribution to the development of their community in some of the other ways I suggest.
Think of the joy that could be brought into the hearts of our senior citizens if on one of those days each Canadian took it upon himself in an organized fashion-members of parliament do this all the time-to go and visit a senior citizens' homes or hospital. I was in a senior citizens' home in my own riding yesterday. One not dedicated to those who can help themselves but to those who cannot help
June 20, 1975

themselves. There was great joy on that occasion; it was a very happy occasion for many people. It was the first time in a long period that any one of those people had seen a group of individuals enjoying themselves. They live their lives in pain, and in many respects in loneliness. Can you imagine the contribution that would be made to the well being of our country and to those unfortunate people in particular if each Canadian agreed in an organized way to give up a holiday, a day in front of the television set or on the golf course, tennis courts, or a day at the cottage, and visited some unfortunate citizen?
I do not know whether any member has had the experience I have had of visiting a hospital and talking to someone I have never met before. The fact that someone is paying attention to that unfortunate person for a few moments is a great experience for him. If each of us did that sort of thing we would bring more joy into the world in one day than we could imagine.
I and my children are fortunate to live in a community where men and women in the community have dedicated themselves and their leisure time to the training of young boys and girls in such mundane things as hockey, football, and softball. They do this in many ways. What a difference it would make to that community if each of us as Canadians showed an interest on that particular day in the young people who are working to excel and to compete in a healthy way. Perhaps we could engage ourselves in an organized manner by getting to know one another in the sense of the differences that exist in our country-people who are different from ourselves, who are newcomers to Canada and who want to make as great a contribution to the country as other people.
I dare say, Mr. Speaker, there could even be a parliamentary appreciation day of some kind. Perhaps that might be worth-while in view of some of the things that have happened over the last little while. I am appalled when I go into schools, and when I speak to organizations, at how little information there is about the operation and importance of this place. I know members of parliament try to occupy themselves in educating our young people, but many Canadians could occupy themselves by coming to this institution or by studying this institution and the provincial institutions in this country.
I have mentioned a number of topics, but if we are going to give ourselves a day off from work I think it is important that it not be a day that is wasted in the sense of our country. A day off from work is never wasted in the sense of ourselves, but it ought to be a day off that is not wasted in terms of our country. If we are to deal with this bill, let us deal with it from the point of view of advancing our community, the people who live in our community, and our worth-while institutions, not from the point of view of just advancing ourselves indirectly.
I should like to hear the views of other members, and I am particularly interested in the views of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) on this matter because of his usual contribution to the debates in this House. I know the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan' has some views on this matter as well.
Canada Labour Code
If we are to give ourselves that extra holiday, which perhaps we need, then I would put it to the members of this House through you, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps our country needs the efforts which are generated on that holiday a lot more than we need the holiday itself.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not find myself in any conflict of interest here this afternoon, and I might say I was very pleased to note the strong support given my bill, C-208, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TWO MORE GENERAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY
speechtext:
The reason I happen to be responding this afternoon has nothing to do with that bill, but rather, since this bill purports to amend the Canada Labour Code, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour it is my duty to speak during this debate.
I do welcome the good intentions and the support of this House for my bill and I hope it will yet receive third reading and pass this place. There is also, I understand, even the possibility that there may be some government initiative in this area which would, in that case, ensure that this holiday would be established in time for the third Monday of February next year.
The mail which I have received on that bill, and undoubtedly other hon. members have received similar letters, would indicate that there is some concern on the part of people in this country, and especially the members of the business community, that we are in the process of establishing too many holidays in Canada. Perhaps they would be more reassured were we not trying to establish them as paid holidays.
Actually the very notion of holidays has aroused some people to very considerable concern at what they consider to be a time when Canadians should be working more rather than less. While I respect that sentiment, I would say that I do not share the feeling. It seems to me that for those who have to work, especially those who work with their hands and their bodies, even as many as one paid holiday a month, some 12, would not be an excessive number.
I would further say, Mr. Speaker, that I see no problem in principle with the bill the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has presented, certainly not for my part and I believe not on the part of the government either. The principle is not in question. All that really is in question is how far we should go by legislation, and what days we should actually pick as the days that should be established as our holidays.
The preliminary data from the 1973 Working Conditions Survey in respect of federal jurisdiction industries indicate that 95 per cent of the employees had nine or more paid general holidays, even though the legislation now requires only eight days. Seventy-nine per cent of employees had 10 or more paid general holidays. In all industries, the percentage of employees having nine paid holidays or more was 84 per cent, and the percentage having 10 or more paid holidays was 62 per cent.
June 20, 1975

Canada Labour Code
In 1973, collective agreement data show that 92 per cent of all employees in federal jurisdiction industries, and 85 per cent of all employees in all industries, received nine or more paid holidays. Seventy-three per cent of all employees in federal jurisdiction and 72 per cent of all employees in all industries received 10 or more paid holidays.
The above data thus show that a large majority of employees receive nine holidays or more in a year, while the number receiving 10 holidays or more has increased and now reflects a majority. It will be realized, of course, that the nine holidays enjoyed by the majority differs from province to province and even from employer to employer. The bill presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre leaves some room for the substitution of one holiday for another in cases where the collective agreement would make that substitution.
The impressive percentage of Canadian employees, some 72 per cent, who already have 10 or more paid holidays indicates that this legislation would not be driving us very far beyond the norm that has now come to be accepted in collective bargaining in this country.
This is not the first time, of course, the hon. member has presented us with such legislation in this House. He has been carrying out a good role in bringing it before the House over the years. I think in every session of parliament he presents identically the same bill, or one very close to it, and I have no doubt that perhaps on some occasion, perhaps even today, it will be rewarded with second reading, and eventually perhaps even passage.
In the present situation, as the hon. member has indicated, the Canada Labour Code provides for eight general holidays with pay. This standard came into effect in 1965, some 10 years ago. Perhaps it may now be thought that this lapse of 10 years is enough time for us to reconsider the legislative requirement.
When we compare the proposal before us with provincial legislation we see that not all the provinces have similar legislation. Some provinces lay down requirements requiring pay for work done on public holidays and, among those that do, some require different numbers of holidays, not all with exactly the same figure. Some require the payment of overtime for work done on a number of public holidays.
In some other countries, such as the United States, I believe the matter of general holidays is still left to the process of collective bargaining, and this question is one of the matters, appropriately a most basic matter of principle, that ought to be applied to a bill of this kind. But in light of the fact that the Canada Labour Code already recognizes that there should be a minimum number of paid working days, I think that would not be a substantial objection to legislation of this kind in Canada.
We do now have a guarantee of eight days, and I think the real question we should consider at this point is whether the days which are proposed in Bill C-249 are the ones which are most aptly added. Considering the fact that the hon. member's bill provides for the substitution of some days, I suppose there is not really a problem here of very great difficulty.

It should be noted that many collective bargaining agreements provide for the celebration of Boxing Day as a holiday, probably many more than provide for the establishment of a day in February, which is the preferred date certainly in my own bill. I take it that is also the wish of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) expressed a very strong admonition in respect of how we should observe our holidays. I think we would all agree with him that Canadians ought to celebrate their holidays in a very worthwhile fashion, but I would hesitate to suggest that this House lay down in legislative principle that Canadians should do such and such on a particular holiday, and I did not really take the hon. member to be suggesting something of that kind. He did speak of the many good things that Canadians might do on holidays, which we on this side trust that Canadians are doing every day, as are we ourselves, and as the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton indicated he was doing. I think probably that kind of consideration is one which is best left to the good judgment of Canadians and their generosity, rather than legislated in a bill of this kind.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did not specify a particular date in February. If the Heritage Day legislation were followed, it would be the third Monday in February. The justification for having a celebration at that time is not only the chronological one, that it is the time of the year when there is a long break between holidays, but also that it is a very appropriate time to celebrate our national heritage.
Obviously there are some links between a holiday in February, at least the concept of that holiday as the national Heritage Day, and our Dominion Day, or Canada Day, or whatever name we decide to give it. In a sense both holidays cover the same ground, but Heritage Day in particular reflects the diversity of our people. It indicates the fact that Canadians come to this country with different heritages. The heritage that is to be celebrated is the collective heritage. While we have many points in common, there are also obviously many points of difference between us. This should be drawn to the attention of the Canadian people through the proclamation of that particular day.
I might add that one of the thoughts in my mind in proposing that day as a holiday was the feeling that it would be better if it were held some time during the school year. I recall that during my days in school we prepared for every significant holiday with concerts which would be staged, and young people were taught about the particular day for which they were preparing, whether it was Empire Day or Victoria Day. I would similarly envisage Heritage Day in February, being long enough after Christmas to allow grade school students, with the assistance of their teachers, to prepare colourful programs for that day. Of course, the appropriate time of the year for such activities by school children is when school is in session.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre himself supports that day or a day about that time, as well as a
June 20, 1975

holiday in August which I think is probably celebrated in the majority of provinces.
There remains the vexing question of what to do about Boxing Day and whether or not it would not be more appropriate as one of the paid holidays than the days that are to be proclaimed. However, my own view is that, since we are merely establishing a minimum here, if other collective agreements wished to provide that Boxing Day or any other day or days would also be proclaimed as paid holidays, there would be no conflict because it would simply be an additional day to be added to the minimum number of days which are provided for here.
So I am happy to say that I am in agreement with the bill proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I could support that bill if it should come to a vote this afternoon, and I hope that the fact that he has drawn this need to our attention again, if it does not result in success at this time through his legislative efforts, will again remind the government and the people that this is an area in which further legislation is necessary for the benefit of the working men and women of our country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TWO MORE GENERAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this chance to speak on a subject that is very important to me and that has been important for many years before I came here. In this life of high pressure we can hardly call this a debate. It is rather a dialogue on something we agree is essential.
I suspect that the principle behind this bill will cause less argument than the debates and names of the holidays. I am sure we will argue over the date on which a holiday should fall and about the name which should be given to it. I would like to suggest-and I will probably get into an argument over this-that perhaps the first Monday in December should be proclaimed a holiday in order to prepare for the pressure of another holiday, the Yuletide vacation. I say that lightly, but, as you know, winter time is the time in life when you need rest most, when the days seem long at times and the months drag on.
I do support very strongly a February holiday. Having been in industry and having been a negotiator of trade union contracts, I can say that we have negotiated this in many contracts across the country. My own guild has searched for a holiday time and has decided that a paid holiday should be set. Since there was no other appropriate time, it was decided that everybody's birthday would become a paid holiday.
I would certainly welcome a break in mid winter, in February, when rest is essential. We need that time to rest
Canada Labour Code
from the heavy stress and long months. In fact in industry they are now talking about shorter weeks of work to achieve greater production. They have found that the mind is more alert, people survive on the job better and are more productive when they work only three or four days a week. It seems to me that if industry were realistic it would welcome an extra holiday in order to increase productivity, however slightly, which would result from a rest during winter.
As to the summer time, I am not very excited about a summer holiday because most of us find a way to enjoy it.
